newsitem.title: USA: Al Gore -- Clinton's Democratic heir apparent.
newsitem.headline: Al Gore -- Clinton's Democratic heir apparent.

text.p: Al Gore has made quite a record as an influential, globe-trotting U.S. vice president and alter ego to Bill Clinton -- and that is only one sign he may be preparing to run for president in the year 2000.
More significant may be the increasingly popular Al Gore comedy routines out on the speaking circuit, where he lampoons his own reputation for scholarly dullness and wooden demeanor.
He tells jokes on himself deadpan. He pretends to dance the Macarena standing stock still. He was once wheeled up to a lectern on a train porter's luggage cart, rigid as a statue.
Audiences love it. And it is an axiom of American politics that when politicians start making fun of their own shortcomings, they are preparing for a big career move.
For Albert Arnold Gore Jr, 48, former Democratic senator from Tennessee, that could only be Bill Clinton's job.

Clinton, seeking a second and final four-year term, has aided Gore's cause first by choosing him as a running mate in 1992 and then by giving him assignments and influence far beyond what predecessors enjoyed in a largely ceremonial post.
Gore is what Clinton is not: The son of a former Washington insider -- his father was also a senator from Tennessee -- and bred to the ways of the U.S. capital from boyhood on.

But he and the president also share Ivy League backgrounds -- Gore is Harvard, Clinton is Yale Law -- and hail from the next-door southern states of Tennessee and Arkansas. Both are brainy and fascinated by the details of policy and politics.
Accordingly, Gore and Clinton have developed an unusually close relationship for men in their very unequal positions.
Clinton calls Gore the best U.S. vice president ever, and says he chose him because "I wanted someone smarter than me."
Gore, who is a very private man despite his very public role, will not discuss their relationship in any detail except to credit Clinton for vastly expanding his duties.

In an interview with Reuters last year, Gore said, "The main difference (in this White House relationship) is his generosity, his self-confidence in feeling comfortable enough to ask me to play a significant role and the friendship that we share, which is very real and very enjoyable."
When it was noted that many presidents had promised their number-two would have significant roles, Gore replied, "This time it really has happened. What you see is what you get."

White House officials say he has become Clinton's closest confidant and an ardent advocate of the "sensible center" in political matters, especially since the departure last summer of top political strategist Dick Morris due to a sex scandal.
Gore's areas of expertise range from the environment and technology to foreign policy.
He has been Clinton's emissary on a number of foreign trips. When Russian President Boris Yeltsin was re-elected in June, Gore was the first senior U.S. official to see him.
During that July visit, Gore also pressed for an end to the renewed fighting in Chechnya, which Washington feared was eroding support for Yeltsin around the world.

Gore was born in Washington on March 31, 1948 and lived much of his youth in an apartment in a ritzy Washington hotel with his parents, including then-Sen. Albert Gore Sr of Tennessee, and his older sister.
Gore's father, a devotee of President Franklin Roosevelt's liberal "New Deal" government-fostered social policies, served in Congress from 1939 to 1970.
Young Al attended elite St. Albans prep school, graduated from Harvard and attended divinity school at Vanderbilt University in Tennessee before switching to its law school.
He is married to the former "Tipper" Aitcheson, whose crusade in the 1980s against obscene rock lyrics once made her more famous than her husband. They have four children.
